=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's Package

**Scope note:** I reviewed the full Seller Update and Disclosure Letter, including items labelled [STANDARD]. The Seller's labels are its own characterisation, and nothing in the package shows the Buyer has agreed them. Several [STANDARD] items are among the most buyer-adverse terms here. The "FINAL / not to be re-opened" language also doesn't bind the Buyer, so I've treated every position as open. I've worked from the Seller's summary, not the full SPA text, so the clause cross-references need checking against the actual draft.

## 1. The general liability and recovery package is seller-favourable

- **Cap (cl 12.1): 20% of price (AUD 4.8m).** This is the top of the range the Seller itself describes. The "market context" is the Seller's assertion, not evidence, so benchmark it against our own precedent and deal data before accepting it. The cap is also small relative to the known exposures (see section 3).
- **Thresholds (cl 12.2): AUD 25k de minimis and AUD 250k excess-only basket.** The basket works as a deductible: the Buyer recovers nothing until claims reach AUD 250k, and then only the excess. The de minimis means small claims don't count toward the basket at all. Push for a tipping basket (first-dollar recovery once exceeded), a lower basket, and a de minimis that counts toward the basket.
- **Time limits (cl 12.3/13): 18 months for general warranties.** 18 months is short for a SaaS business with a Bluefen revenue dependency and an open data incident. It also falls before a full audit cycle covering tax, so the tax and IP claim periods need to run longer.

## 2. Fundamental warranties, tax and IP are being pulled into the general regime

- **Title and capacity (Fundamental).** The Seller proposes the same caps and time limits as general warranties "for administrative simplicity." This should be rejected. Title and capacity warranties should be uncapped (or capped at price), with a claim period of at least 6 years, which is the NSW limitation default for contract claims under the *Limitation Act 1969* (NSW). Confirm the position for this SPA.
- **Tax.** Tax warranties and indemnities should sit outside the general cap and basket, with a claim period at least matching the ATO amendment period (generally 4 years from lodgement, longer in some cases).
- **IP.** The Seller says the IP warranties are "settled under the general regime." They aren't settled from the Buyer's side. Given the Ironquay issue, IP ownership should be a fundamental warranty.
- **Scope of limitations (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5).** These apply to "all Claims of any nature," which would reach fraud and fundamental claims. Carve out fraud (which cannot be contractually excluded as against the fraudster), fundamental warranties, tax, and specific indemnities. Confirm with NSW counsel how far the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance wording reaches misleading conduct.

## 3. Buyer knowledge and general disclosure would gut the warranties

- **General data-room disclosure (Schedule 7 / DL 1.1–1.2).** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room, including the public registers, would mean nearly every problem found in diligence is disclosed against the warranties. The Buyer would then have no warranty claim for matters it found, and the warranties would be largely hollow. Reject. Disclosure should be specific, fair, and against a specific warranty.
- **Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3).** This bars claims for anything the Buyer or its advisers knew, including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records. Combined with the general disclosure, this is effectively an anti-sandbagging clause plus a constructive-knowledge test. Delete it, and add an express pro-sandbagging clause so the Buyer's knowledge doesn't reduce its warranty rights. Australian law on sandbagging is not settled, so the express wording matters.

## 4. Known issues are being pushed into warranties, where they don't belong

The Seller's documents identify several known matters. Known matters should be handled by price, conditions, or specific indemnities, not by warranty claims that the cap, basket, and knowledge clause would defeat.

| Item | Seller position | Problem | Buyer pushback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bluefen** (~30% of FY26 revenue, AUD 3.6m) | Reasonable endeavours; consent "satisfied" on delivery of counterparty consent (cl 3 / 6.3) | No consent yet. The Seller's trigger ignores the conditions in cl 11.3. | Make consent a condition precedent. Require the Seller to deliver consent *and* evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. Add a long-stop date with a walk right. Consider an escrow or price adjustment if consent comes with conditions. |
| **Riverlark** (AUD 3.2m outstanding) | Release "to be provided following Completion" (cl 2 / 7) | Under a debt-free/cash-free deal, this debt must be paid from the price at Completion. A post-Completion release leaves the Company exposed to the bank's security and the Buyer funding the repayment. | Require payoff at Completion from the sale proceeds, with a payoff letter and discharge of security delivered at Completion. Deduct the amount from the equity price. |
| **Ironquay IP** (AUD 180k open on SOW3) | Indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment; "considered adequate" (cl 11.1) | The Company may not own the SOW3 Project Materials until fees are paid (DD-004 cl 7.3), and no confirmatory assignment exists. The indemnity is too narrow. | Pay the AUD 180k pre-Completion or treat it as a debt-like item. Require a confirmatory assignment as a condition. Give a broad specific indemnity for all Ironquay claims, and a fundamental IP ownership warranty. |
| **Employee bonuses** (AUD 420k) | Seller's matter; not in the funds flow (DD-005) | Real cost to the Company, not reflected in price. Payroll tax and superannuation/on-costs are not addressed. | Treat as a debt-like item deducted from price, including all employer on-costs (NSW payroll tax and superannuation, at current rates to be verified). Seller bears any Completion bonus payable on conditions it controls. |
| **Supplier renewals** (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k) | "Ordinary-course operating costs" | The three renewals appear to be timed and scoped together, and it is unclear whether they are unavoidable or terminable. "Ordinary course" is not a pricing answer. | Require the Seller to confirm each renewal's terms, termination rights and accrual status. Any committed post-Completion cost not reflected in working capital should be a price adjustment. |
| **Office lease** (DD-007) | Notification obligation only | Landlord consent to a change of control has not been ruled out. | Require confirmation (or a landlord waiver) that no consent is needed, or make consent a condition. |
| **Mossvale** (DD-009) | Restriction on assignment noted | Unclear whether a share sale triggers the restriction. | Require written confirmation from Mossvale, or treat it as a CP if consent is needed. |

## 5. The privacy incident is the most serious undisclosed-risk item

DD-006 records a download link sent to an unintended external email address. The export may contain about 1,240 records, including names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." That isn't a basis for the Buyer to accept any risk.

Key points:
- Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), if the Company suspects an eligible data breach, it must carry out a reasonable and expeditious assessment, generally within 30 days. If that clock is running, the timing is urgent. Establish the date of the incident and the status of the assessment now.
- Whether notification to the OAIC and affected individuals is required, and the cost of any response, are unknown.

Push for:
- A pre-Completion forensic review and a written NDB assessment, with the Buyer's input on any notifications.
- A specific indemnity for all costs, claims, regulatory action and notification costs arising from the incident, outside the cap and basket, with a claim period of several years.
- A data protection warranty, and an escrow or retention until the assessment is closed.

## 6. Title and funds flow

- **Title (DD-012):** The share register showing Harbourglass as holder is one source, not verification. Require an ASIC company extract, original share certificates, a PPSR search, and a warranty that the shares are free of encumbrances. Title should be fundamental (see section 2).
- **Funds flow:** It reflects "agreed price mechanics," but it omits the bonuses and does not show the Riverlark payoff. Do not accept it until it reflects every debt-like item.

## 7. Recommendations (summary)

1. **Reject the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing and the instruction to review only [OPEN] items.** Review and mark up every clause.
2. **Delete general data-room disclosure** (Schedule 7, DL 1.1–1.2). Disclosure must be specific.
3. **Delete the buyer-knowledge bar** (cl 8.3) and add an express pro-sandbagging clause.
4. **Raise the general cap** above 20% (or push for a higher figure, with market evidence), and convert the excess-only basket to a tipping basket with a lower threshold.
5. **Extend the general claim period** to at least 24–36 months, with tax at ATO-matched periods.
6. **Carve out fundamental warranties (title, capacity, IP ownership), tax, fraud and specific indemnities** from the cap, basket, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions.
7. **Make Bluefen consent a condition precedent**, with a long-stop date and walk right.
8. **Require Riverlark payoff and security discharge at Completion**, deducted from price.
9. **Resolve Ironquay**: pay or deduct the AUD 180k, obtain a confirmatory IP assignment as a CP, and give a broad specific indemnity.
10. **Treat the AUD 420k bonuses and on-costs as debt-like items** deducted from price.
11. **Get the supplier renewal terms** and resolve their accrual and working-capital treatment.
12. **Require a forensic review, NDB assessment and specific privacy indemnity** for DD-006.
13. **Confirm lease and Mossvale consent position** in writing, or make consent a CP.
14. **Verify title** independently of the share register.

**Known-exposure check:** Bluefen (AUD 3.6m revenue at risk, valuation impact to be modelled), Riverlark (AUD 3.2m debt), Ironquay (AUD 180k), bonuses (AUD 420k) and supplier renewals (AUD 330k) total about AUD 4.13m in quantifiable items before on-costs, privacy exposure and any Bluefen impact. That already approaches the Seller's general cap, and the cap is not designed to cover known matters. These should be dealt with as price adjustments, conditions or specific indemnities, not warranty claims.

**Caveats:** This is a first-pass review based on the Seller's summary, not the full SPA. The NSW limitation periods, Privacy Act timing, payroll tax and superannuation rates, and the ATO amendment period should be confirmed by NSW counsel and the tax advisers before the mark-up goes out.
